input: Compile a reading list on behavioral economics

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Behavioral economics is broad — knowing whether to include foundational theory, nudge policy, consumer behavior, finance applications, or all of these shapes which titles make the cut.
Whether this list is for the user themselves, a student, a team, or a general audience determines the assumed baseline knowledge and relevance of titles.
The desired length of the list affects how selective to be — a top-5 essentials list is curated very differently from a comprehensive 30-book syllabus.
The balance between academic papers/textbooks vs. accessible popular books (e.g., Thinking, Fast and Slow vs. journal articles) determines the tone and usability of the list.
Knowing the purpose — self-improvement, academic study, professional application, or teaching — anchors which angles of behavioral economics to prioritize.
Whether the list should be annotated with summaries/reasons to read, or just titles and authors, changes the effort and format of the final deliverable significantly.
The desired format (plain list, spreadsheet, organized by theme/difficulty, etc.) and where it will live determines how to structure and deliver the output.

gold.taskTitle: Compile a behavioral economics reading list
gold.taskDescription: Curate a structured list of reading materials focused on behavioral economics for a specific purpose and audience.

questions.title: Which topics within behavioral economics should be covered?
questions.description: Determine whether the list should focus on a specific area (e.g., nudge theory, cognitive biases, financial decision-making) or cover the field broadly.

questions.title: Who is this reading list being made for?
questions.description: Identify the intended reader — the user personally, a student, a professional team, or a broader audience — to calibrate assumed knowledge level.

questions.title: What is the purpose behind building this list?
questions.description: Clarify the use case — self-study, a university course, workplace training, a research project — to anchor which titles are most relevant.

questions.title: How many titles should the final list include?
questions.description: Establish a target number to determine how selective or comprehensive the curation needs to be.

questions.title: Should it lean toward popular books or academic texts?
questions.description: Decide the preferred balance between accessible non-fiction (e.g., Ariely, Thaler) and academic papers, textbooks, or journal articles.

questions.title: Should each title include an annotation or description?
questions.description: Determine whether the list needs summaries, reading rationale, or difficulty ratings alongside each entry, or just titles and authors.

questions.title: What format should the final reading list be delivered in?
questions.description: Clarify the desired output format — plain text, a document, organized by theme or difficulty level, spreadsheet, etc.
